read: partial: pp. 1-16 (abstract, 1 introduction, 2 problem and methods, 3 results, 4 discussion, 5 related work, 6 conclusion) in full; appendices B (data annotation), C, D and E (pp. 25-28) read; example tables (pp. 17-24, 29) and reference list skimmed
venue_now: arXiv 2211.14275v1, 25 Nov 2022 (DeepMind preprint dated 2022-11-28, p. 1); the text shows no venue. The search note mentions a NeurIPS 2022 MATH-AI workshop version; neither it nor I verified it.
what_it_is: A DeepMind study, not a benchmark, comparing outcome-based supervision (final-answer correctness) with process-based supervision (GSM8K's human-written reasoning traces as SFT targets, and human step-correctness labels for a process reward model) when fine-tuning a 70B LM on GSM8K (pp. 1-6). It reports final-answer error by exact match and trace error, the share of problems with a correct final answer whose trace contains at least one incorrect step according to human annotators (p. 3). Outcome- and process-based training reach similar final-answer error (23.5% vs 22.3% without a reward model, 16.6% vs 14.8% with one), but low trace error needs process feedback or a reward model that emulates it: 19.8% for few-shot final-answer RL against 11.4% for SFT, and a best of 12.4% for RL against final-answer correctness against 3.8% for the best process-based method (p. 2; Table 1, p. 7; p. 8). Step labels came from humans because the authors 'lack reliable programmatic means for determining the correctness of intermediate steps' (p. 4).
domain: grade-school math word problems (GSM8K); out-of-distribution check on the MATH pre-algebra split (p. 11)
size: GSM8K split into 7,118 train, 256 validation and 1,319 test problems (p. 3); 1,560 human-annotated model samples on 530 problems (9,856 step labels) for PRM training, 162 validation samples with 913 steps, and trace error estimated on 200 correct-answer problems per model for 10 models (p. 6); one 70B base LM (p. 2; Table 1, p. 7)
source_of_items: existing dataset (GSM8K test set: human-written problems and reference solutions); model-generated solutions labelled by trained human annotators
has_gold_traces: partial: GSM8K's human-written reference solutions (SFT targets, shown to annotators; pp. 4, 6) and human first-major-mistake labels on model samples, converted to per-step binary labels (p. 6)
evaluation: final answer (exact string match on integer answers) plus step-level human annotation of answer-correct samples (trace error); also selective-prediction error and OOD error (p. 3)
human_validation: Annotators passed a qualification on solutions where three authors agreed on the first major mistake: 21 of 91 candidates admitted (p. 25). 20% of training problems were doubly labelled and annotators below 75% agreement removed, about 21% of the data (p. 26). After filtering, 92% agreement and Cohen's kappa 0.915 on locating the first incorrect step; on the evaluation set 87% agreement but kappa 0.34 on whole-trace correctness, which the authors attribute to errors behind correct answers being subtler (p. 26). Table 1 gives trace-error ranges by whether one or both raters must flag an error, e.g. 19.8 (7.9-31.7) (p. 7).
contamination_measures: none (public GSM8K test set; own validation split carved from the training set, p. 3)

engtrace_use.explanation: Not cited in the May paper, whose only process-supervision citation is Lightman et al. (2023) (May p. 4). It belongs in the new paragraph on process supervision and judge validity, as the origin, with Lightman et al., of process supervision, and as the source of the trace-error construct (p. 3) that EngTrace's hard case measures: experts found at least one incorrect step in 93 of 228 correct-answer traces (brief sec. 3). Its statement that intermediate steps could not be checked programmatically (p. 4) names the gap that EngTrace's code-derived milestone values fill in its own domain. A careful reviewer of a paper about verifiable process supervision would expect it.

suggested_wording: Process supervision was first compared with outcome supervision by Uesato et al. (2022), who found on GSM8K that training on final answers alone matches process-based training on final-answer error but leaves many more correct answers resting on a flawed step, and who relied on human step labels because intermediate steps could not be checked programmatically.
facts_to_cite: First comprehensive comparison of process- and outcome-based supervision on a natural-language task, GSM8K (abstract, p. 1); the authors call it the first empirical paper on the distinction (p. 13).
Trace error is the fraction of problems with a correct final answer whose solution contains at least one incorrect reasoning step, as judged by human annotators (p. 3).
Outcome- and process-based approaches reach similar final-answer error: 23.5% vs 22.3% without a reward model and 16.6% vs 14.8% with one (p. 2; Table 1, p. 7).

Trace error is higher under outcome supervision: 19.8% for Few-shot+Final-Answer RL against 11.4% for SFT; the best model trained by RL against final-answer correctness reaches 12.4% against 3.8% for the best process-based method (p. 2; Table 1, p. 7; p. 8).

The best overall system lowers trace error among answer-correct solutions from the prior 14.0% (few-shot PaLM-540B) to 3.4% (SFT+ORM-RL with ORM reranking), and final-answer error from 16.8% to 12.7% (abstract, p. 1; Table 1, p. 7).

Reward models trained only on outcome labels agree more with the process labels than with their own outcome labels (85% vs 77% over all steps), which the authors caution may be specific to math (p. 8).

Step labels came from humans because no reliable programmatic check of intermediate steps was available; a heuristic that string-matches intermediate results (Li et al., 2022) did slightly worse (pp. 4, 9).
On the evaluation set, raters agreed 87% on whole-trace correctness with Cohen's kappa 0.34, lower than on training data because errors behind correct answers are subtler (p. 26).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares the core measurement, whether a correct final answer rests on a correct trace (p. 3), with human step labels as ground truth. Lacks: generated instances (static GSM8K); an engineering domain (grade-school math); gold intermediate values (it has human reference solutions and human labels, p. 4); any evaluation of an evaluator against labels of the kind EngTrace runs on PRMs and judges (it trains reward models). Its human labels are noisy on exactly the hard case (kappa 0.34 on answer-correct traces, p. 26), where EngTrace reports Fleiss kappa 0.781 on steps from three own-branch experts (brief sec. 3). The constructs differ: Uesato counts the first major mistake, 'a step where the information expressed is incorrect, or it would no longer be possible to reach the correct solution without undoing that step' (p. 6), while EngTrace's 178 incorrect steps in correct-answer traces are mostly calculation slips (175 of 178), in traces the experts' holistic verdict called sound in 90 of 93 cases (PILOT_SUMMARY sec. 2.5). The two rates should not be compared as like for like.
notes: Internal inconsistency in the paper: the conclusion (pp. 15-16) attributes the 3.4% trace error to 'SFT with PRM reranking', gives its outcome-based analogue 12.7% trace error, and reports a reduction 'from 12.7% to 5.5%'; Table 1 (p. 7) gives 3.5% for SFT with PRM reranking, 3.4% for SFT+ORM-RL, 12.4% for Few-shot+Final-Answer RL with ORM reranking, and p. 8 says 12.4% to 5.5%. Cite Table 1. The catalogue's 'trace error among answer-correct solutions cut from 14.0% to 3.4% only with process supervision' is imprecise: 14.0% is the prior state of the art from few-shot prompting, not an outcome-supervised arm, and the 3.4% system uses an outcome-trained reward model on top of process-based SFT (Table 1, p. 7). The model is DeepMind's own 70B base LM (Hoffmann et al., 2022; p. 2). Lightman et al. (2023), already cited, is the companion reference.
